## Problem 1

### a
```{r}
momentum_walk1 <- function(n, p) {
  if (length(n) != 1 || !is.numeric(n) || is.na(n) ||
      n < 1 || n != floor(n)) {
    stop("n must be a positive integer.")
  }

  if (length(p) != 1 || !is.numeric(p) || is.na(p) ||
      p < 0 || p > 1) {
    stop("p must be between 0 and 1.")
  }

  directions <- rbind(
    right = c(1, 0),
    left  = c(-1, 0),
    up    = c(0, 1),
    down  = c(0, -1)
  )

  current_dir <- sample(1:4, 1)
  position <- directions[current_dir, ]

  if (n >= 2) {
    for (i in 2:n) {
      if (runif(1) >= p) {
        current_dir <- sample(1:4, 1)
      }
      position <- position + directions[current_dir, ]
    }
  }

  return(as.numeric(position))
}
```

### b
```{r}
momentum_walk2 <- function(n, p) {
  if (length(n) != 1 || !is.numeric(n) || is.na(n) ||
      n < 1 || n != floor(n)) {
    stop("n must be a positive integer.")
  }

  if (length(p) != 1 || !is.numeric(p) || is.na(p) ||
      p < 0 || p > 1) {
    stop("p must be between 0 and 1.")
  }

  directions <- rbind(
    right = c(1, 0),
    left  = c(-1, 0),
    up    = c(0, 1),
    down  = c(0, -1)
  )

  current_dir <- sample(1:4, 1)

  steps <- sapply(seq_len(n), function(i) {
    if (i > 1 && runif(1) >= p) {
      current_dir <<- sample(1:4, 1)
    }
    directions[current_dir, ]
  })

  return(as.numeric(rowSums(steps)))
}
```

Now we run the test to see the outcome

```{r}
momentum_walk1(10, 0.6)
momentum_walk2(10, 0.6)

momentum_walk1(1000, 0.6)
momentum_walk2(1000, 0.6)
```

momentum_walk1() uses a for loop to generate the walk sequentially. At each step after the first, the previous direction is preserved with probability p; otherwise a new direction is sampled uniformly from the four possible directions. momentum_walk2() implements the same sequential update using sapply() and sums the resulting displacement vectors to obtain the final position.

### c

```{r}
set.seed(506)
momentum_walk1(10, 0.6)

set.seed(506)
momentum_walk1(10, 0.6)

set.seed(506)
momentum_walk1(1000, 0.6)

set.seed(506)
momentum_walk1(1000, 0.6)
```

I used set.seed(506) before each simulation. Setting the same seed resets R's random-number generator to the same initial state, so the same sequence of random numbers is generated and the simulation produces the same final position.

### d

```{r}
set.seed(506)

p_values <- c(0, 0.5, 0.9)

final_positions <- sapply(
  p_values,
  function(p) momentum_walk1(1000, p)
)

distances <- sqrt(colSums(final_positions^2))

data.frame(
  p = p_values,
  distance = distances
)
```

In these three simulations, the final distance generally tends to be larger for higher momentum. However, since each value of p is represented by only one random walk, these individual simulations are not sufficient to determine typical behavior.

### e

```{r}
set.seed(506)

p_values <- c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 0.9)

mean_distances <- sapply(p_values, function(p) {

  distances <- replicate(1000, {
    pos <- momentum_walk1(1000, p)
    sqrt(sum(pos^2))
  })

  mean(distances)
})

mc_results <- data.frame(
  p = p_values,
  mean_distance = mean_distances
)

mc_results
```

The mean final distance increases as p increases. Higher momentum makes consecutive steps more persistent in the same direction, so the walk tends to travel farther from its starting point.

### f

```{r}
library(microbenchmark)

bench_1000 <- microbenchmark(
  loop = momentum_walk1(1000, 0.6),
  apply = momentum_walk2(1000, 0.6),
  times = 100
)

bench_1000

bench_100000 <- microbenchmark(
  loop = momentum_walk1(100000, 0.6),
  apply = momentum_walk2(100000, 0.6),
  times = 10
)

bench_100000
```

momentum_walk1 was faster for both input sizes. The absolute difference became larger for \(n=100000\), likely because sapply() introduces additional function-call and intermediate-object overhead.

## Problem 2

```{r}
set.seed(506)

n_days <- 10000

morning <- rowSums(matrix(
  rpois(n_days * 3, lambda = 4),
  nrow = n_days
))

peak_morning <- rnorm(
  n_days, mean = 45, sd = 4
)

midday <- rowSums(matrix(
  rpois(n_days * 6, lambda = 15),
  nrow = n_days
))

peak_afternoon <- rnorm(
  n_days, mean = 55, sd = 5
)

evening <- rowSums(matrix(
  rpois(n_days * 6, lambda = 9),
  nrow = n_days
))

daily_total <- morning + peak_morning +
               midday + peak_afternoon + evening

mean(daily_total)
```

Based on 10,000 simulated days, the estimated expected number of passengers per day is approximately 256.1777. This is close to 256 passengers per day.

## Problem 3

```{r}
youtube <- read.csv(
  "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rfordatascience/tidytuesday/master/data/2021/2021-03-02/youtube.csv"
)

names(youtube)

dim(youtube)
```

```{r}
youtube_clean <- youtube[, !names(youtube) %in% c(
  "brand",
  "superbowl_ads_dot_com_url",
  "youtube_url",
  "id",
  "kind",
  "etag",
  "published_at",
  "title",
  "description",
  "thumbnail",
  "channel_title",
  "category_id"
)]

dim(youtube_clean)
names(youtube_clean)
```

I removed variables that could directly identify a particular commercial, including the brand, URLs, video identifiers and metadata, publication information, title, description, thumbnail, and channel information. The resulting dataset has 247 observations and 13 variables.

### b

```{r}
outcomes <- c(
  "view_count",
  "like_count",
  "dislike_count",
  "favorite_count",
  "comment_count"
)

par(mfrow = c(2, 3))

for (v in outcomes) {
  hist(
    youtube_clean[[v]],
    main = v,
    xlab = v
  )
}

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))

summary(youtube_clean[outcomes])
```

```{r}
sapply(youtube_clean[outcomes], function(x) {
  c(
    min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    zeros = sum(x == 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    missing = sum(is.na(x))
  )
})
```

```{r}
youtube_clean$log_view_count <- log1p(youtube_clean$view_count)
youtube_clean$log_like_count <- log1p(youtube_clean$like_count)
youtube_clean$log_dislike_count <- log1p(youtube_clean$dislike_count)
youtube_clean$log_comment_count <- log1p(youtube_clean$comment_count)
```

view_count, like_count, dislike_count, and comment_count are highly right-skewed, so I classified them as category 2 and applied \(\log(1+x)\). favorite_count has no variation among its observed values, so I classified it as category 3.

### c

```{r}
outcomes <- c(
  "log_view_count",
  "log_like_count",
  "log_dislike_count",
  "log_comment_count"
)

# Seven binary characteristics
characteristics <- c(
  "funny",
  "show_product_quickly",
  "patriotic",
  "celebrity",
  "danger",
  "animals",
  "use_sex"
)

# Fit one model for each outcome-characteristic combination
results_list <- lapply(outcomes, function(outcome) {

  outcome_results <- lapply(characteristics, function(characteristic) {

    # Construct regression formula:
    # outcome ~ characteristic + year
    formula_i <- as.formula(
      paste(outcome, "~", characteristic, "+ year")
    )

    # Fit linear regression
    fit_i <- lm(formula_i, data = youtube_clean)

    # Extract coefficient table
    coef_table <- summary(fit_i)$coefficients

    # The second row corresponds to the binary characteristic
    data.frame(
      outcome = outcome,
      characteristic = characteristic,
      estimate = coef_table[2, "Estimate"],
      p_value = coef_table[2, "Pr(>|t|)"],
      stringsAsFactors = FALSE
    )
  })

  do.call(rbind, outcome_results)
})

# Combine all results into one data frame
results <- do.call(rbind, results_list)

# Remove row names for cleaner output
rownames(results) <- NULL

# Display all regression results
results

# Statistically significant associations at alpha = 0.05
significant_results <- results[
  !is.na(results$p_value) & results$p_value < 0.05,
]

significant_results

# Results for view count only
view_results <- results[
  results$outcome == "log_view_count",
]

# Sort by p-value
view_results_sorted <- view_results[
  order(view_results$p_value),
]

view_results_sorted

# Characteristic with the largest positive estimated
# association with view count
largest_positive_view <- view_results[
  which.max(view_results$estimate),
]

largest_positive_view

# Characteristic with the smallest p-value for view count
smallest_p_view <- view_results[
  which.min(view_results$p_value),
]

smallest_p_view

best_characteristic <- smallest_p_view$characteristic

best_characteristic
```

None of the commercial characteristics were significantly associated with the four outcomes at \(\alpha=0.05\). For log view count, danger had the largest positive coefficient (0.667), although it was not significant (\(p=0.094\)).

### d


```{r}
d_data <- youtube_clean[
  complete.cases(
    youtube_clean$log_view_count,
    youtube_clean$danger,
    youtube_clean$year
  ),
]

y <- d_data$log_view_count

X <- cbind(
  intercept = 1,
  danger = as.numeric(d_data$danger),
  year = d_data$year
)

beta_hat <- solve(
  t(X) %*% X,
  t(X) %*% y
)

beta_hat
```

```{r}
fit_lm <- lm(
  log_view_count ~ danger + year,
  data = d_data
)

coef(fit_lm)
```

```{r}
cbind(
  matrix_algebra = as.numeric(beta_hat),
  lm = as.numeric(coef(fit_lm))
)

all.equal(
  as.numeric(beta_hat),
  as.numeric(coef(fit_lm)),
  tolerance = 1e-10
)
```

danger had the smallest p-value for log view count in part (c). Using \(\hat\beta=(X^TX)^{-1}X^Ty\), the estimated coefficients matched those from lm() up to numerical precision.
